segments: ... and sent thirty {OCR?} camel loads
to [Sayf] al-Din,
and showed submission by gifts and other things.
Yet, he was afraid of him.
And after oaths,
when Sayf al-Din went to Syria,
Nur al-Din came to him.
And when they met each other,
Nur al-Din dismounted and kissed the ground before his brother.
And that Sayf al-Din also dismounted,
and they embraced each other and wept.
And Sayf al-Din said to Nur al-Din:
"Why were you not coming to me?
Were you perhaps afraid of me? Believe me, my brother,
that the thought you imagined never entered my mind.
And for what purpose would life and lands be of any use to me,
if I do evil to my brother?" And so, when they were reconciled with each other,
each one returned to his own territory.
And at that time, when Zengi was killed,
Bohemond (Raymond?), the lord of Antioch, marched out to the territory of Aleppo and of Hama,
and made a great slaughter among the Arabs.
And when he took much plunder,
Shirkuh overtook him,
and turned back the plunder.
And also Mujir al-Din, the lord of Damascus, went against Baalbek,
and pressed it hard in battle,
and took it from Najm al-Din Ayyub,
the father of Saladin.
And he gave some villages to Najm al-Din,
and brought him with him to Damascus.
And in that same year, which was 1458,
1458 of the Greeks (1146 of our Lord), in the First Tishrin (October),
Joscelin and Baldwin, the lord of Kesoun, came to Edessa.
And at night, Frankish foot soldiers went up by ladders onto two towers by means of an arrangement they had made with some of the Armenians guarding the wall;
and the Turks fled to the citadel.
And in the morning the Water Gate was opened,
and Joscelin entered.
And when the Franks had remained in Edessa for six days,
Nur al-Din attacked them from Aleppo with ten thousand Turks.
Then Joscelin coerced the wretched people of Edessa,
and rounded up the men, women, boys, and girls,
and brought them out by force at the second hour of the night.
And when morning dawned,
the Turks overtook them,
raining arrows upon them like hailstones,
and cruelly piercing them.
O the cloud of wrath and the merciless day! O the night of death,
and the morning of Gehenna,
and the day of destruction,
which broke upon the wretched Edessenes, the children of the chaste [city]! For the Frankish horsemen, unable to stand firm before the Turks,
abandoned [them] and fled.
